The Competitive Era and Computer Chess

The first modern international chess tournament was held in London in 1851 and was won by the German player Adolf Anderssen. In 1886, Wilhelm Steinitz defeated Johannes Zukertort in a match widely recognized as the first official World Chess Championship. Steinitz is also remembered for developing positional principles that shaped how the game was understood.

The international chess federation, FIDE (Fédération Internationale des Échecs), was founded in Paris in 1924. It began organizing the Chess Olympiad and, from 1948 onward, took control of the World Championship cycle.

The 1972 World Championship match in Reykjavík between the American Bobby Fischer and the Soviet champion Boris Spassky drew enormous public attention during the Cold War. Fischer won, ending a long period of Soviet dominance of the title.

Computers changed chess profoundly. In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated reigning world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match, the first time a computer beat a world champion under standard tournament conditions. Today, chess engines far exceed human strength and are used by players at every level for training and analysis, while online platforms let millions of people play each day.

How Chess Became the Modern Game

In medieval shatranj, the queen (then called the vizier or fers) could move only one square diagonally, and the bishop (the alfil) could jump exactly two squares diagonally. This made the game slow, and a single match could last for many hours.

Around the late 15th century, in southern Europe, the rules changed dramatically. The queen gained the ability to move any number of squares in any direction, and the bishop gained its modern long diagonal move. Because the new queen was so powerful, the style was sometimes called "mad queen chess." The change made games faster and more aggressive, and it is widely seen as the birth of modern chess.

Other rules took longer to settle. Castling developed in several regional variants before its modern form became standard, and the en passant pawn capture was accepted gradually. Pawn promotion to any piece, rather than only to a queen, also became the norm over time.

The printing press helped spread the new rules. One of the earliest surviving printed chess books is by the Spanish author Luis Ramírez de Lucena, published around 1497, which discussed the new style of play and included chess problems.

The Origins of Chess

Chess is generally believed to have originated in northern India during the Gupta Empire, around the 6th century CE. The early form of the game was called chaturanga, a Sanskrit word meaning "four divisions" of the military: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots. These divisions evolved into the pieces we now know as the pawn, knight, bishop, and rook.

From India, the game spread to Persia, where it became known as shatranj. Persian players introduced the custom of warning an opponent when their king was under attack by saying "shah" (king), and the end of the game was announced with "shah mat," meaning "the king is helpless." This phrase is the origin of the English word "checkmate."

After the Islamic conquest of Persia in the 7th century, shatranj spread throughout the Muslim world. Arab scholars wrote some of the earliest known books on chess strategy and composed chess problems called mansubat. Strong players of this era, such as al-Adli and as-Suli, were celebrated at the courts of the Abbasid caliphs.

Chess reached Europe by the 10th century, arriving through Moorish Spain, Sicily, and trade routes with the Byzantine Empire. By the year 1000 it was being played in many parts of Western Europe, often as a pastime of the nobility.
